source_refs.note: Book p. 25: 'Explanation is given in the figure.' and the four-panel figure (a)-(d). Teaching notes, Exam tip, Key points and Common mistake are ours.

blocks.text: The vertical line test is a method used to determine whether a graph represents a function. A graph represents a function if and only if no vertical line intersects the graph more than once. If any vertical line passes through the graph more than once, it is not a function.
Explanation is given in the figure.

blocks.alt: Four small graphs, each crossed by a vertical line. (a) A wavy curve met by the vertical line at one point: a function. (b) A straight line met at one point: a function. (c) A circle met by the vertical line at two points, one above the other: not a function. (d) An S-shaped curve that doubles back, met by the vertical line at three points: not a function.
blocks.caption: Figure: the vertical line test, (a) a function, (b) a function, (c) not a function, (d) not a function (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why does the test work? Every point on a vertical line \(x = c\) has the same \(x\)-coordinate \(c\). If the line meets the graph at two points \((c, y_{1})\) and \((c, y_{2})\) with \(y_{1} \ne y_{2}\), then the one input \(c\) has two outputs. That breaks the definition of a function (one and only one output for each input).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Reading the four graphs:
(a) The curve rises and falls, but every vertical line meets it at most once. So it is a function. Going up and down is allowed.
(b) A slanting straight line: every vertical line meets it exactly once. A function.
(c) A circle: a vertical line through its middle meets it twice, once on the upper half and once on the lower half. Not a function.
(d) The curve bends back on itself; the vertical line shown meets it three times. Not a function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Example in symbols: the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 25\). For \(x = 3\):
\[9 + y^{2} = 25\]
\[y^{2} = 16\]
\[y = 4 \text{ or } y = -4\]
The vertical line \(x = 3\) meets the circle at \((3, 4)\) and \((3, -4)\): two outputs for the input \(3\). So \(y\) is not a function of \(x\) here. But the upper half alone, \(y = \sqrt{25 - x^{2}}\), passes the test and is a function.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: To apply the test, imagine sliding a vertical ruler from left to right across the graph. If at any position it touches the graph at two or more points, write "not a function" and name the line, e.g. "the line \(x = 3\) cuts the graph at two points". One such line is enough to fail; to pass, no line may cut twice.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A graph is a function if and only if no vertical line meets it more than once.
2. Two meeting points on one vertical line = one input with two outputs.
3. A graph may go up and down and still be a function.
4. Circles and curves that bend back are not graphs of functions of \(x\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using a horizontal line instead of a vertical one. A horizontal line meeting the graph twice only means two inputs share an output, which is allowed for a function.
2. Testing only one vertical line. The test needs every vertical line: one bad line is enough to fail.
3. Thinking a curve that rises and falls cannot be a function.
